Empirical Research Plan  

==============================================================  

1. Identification Strategy  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
Preferred design:  “Difference-in-Discontinuities” (a triple-difference that nests an age-based RDD inside a DiD in time and across provinces).  

Why appropriate  

•	Sharp age 30 rule ⇒ clear running variable (single year of age) and cutoff.  
•	The rule existed only in Québec and vanished abruptly on 1 Aug 1989 ⇒ policy shock in time.  
•	No corresponding age rule anywhere else in Canada ⇒ other provinces furnish an external control for nation-wide age-specific trends and macro shocks.  

The estimator compares the discontinuity at age 30 just before the reform with the (zero) discontinuity after the reform, differencing out any smooth age-or-time effects visible in the rest of Canada (ROC). It combines the transparency of an RDD with the power of a DiD and is feasible with the 1986 and 1991 Census master files plus monthly LFS data for dynamic checks.  

Formally:

τ̂ = [(ΔQC,Pre − ΔQC,Post) − (ΔROC,Pre − ΔROC,Post)]  

where Δ = outcome(age ≥ 30) − outcome(age < 30) within a narrow window (e.g. 27–33).  

2. Treatment and Control  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
•	High social-assistance entitlement created by being (i) in Québec, (ii) under the pre-1989 regime, and (iii) at least 30 years old.  

Control groups  
•	Primary: Québec men aged 27–29 and 30–33 observed after the benefit gap is abolished.  
•	Secondary: Same age groups in the rest of Canada, 1986 & 1991.  

Treatment timing  
•	Policy in force: 1 Jan 1969 – 31 Jul 1989.  
•	Policy abolished: 1 Aug 1989 (so 1991 Census = post).  

Running variable  
•	Single year of age (integer 25…39).  
•	Cutoff: 30th birthday. Operates mechanically; cannot be manipulated by respondents.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes in age.  
 Labour-market outcomes would evolve smoothly over age absent the policy; any jump exactly at 30 in Québec pre-1989 is attributable to the benefit schedule.  
 Plausibility: Biological and labour-market determinants of work evolve gradually; census age is as-reported DOB, hard to manipulate.  

A2. Stable age difference over time in absence of reform (local parallel trends).  
 The age-30 discontinuity in Québec would have remained constant between 1986 and 1991 if the rule had stayed.  
 Plausibility: Short interval (5 yrs) and narrow age bands reduce cohort effects; corroborated by ROC placebo.  

A3. No Québec-specific shocks at age 30 coinciding with 1989.  
 Other policy changes must not target the same group at exactly the same time.  
 Plausibility: Québec’s 1988–91 reforms of UI, health coverage, etc. did not hinge on age 30. We will verify in statutes.  

A4. No spillovers across provinces or ages (SUTVA).  
 The rule pertains only to Québec residents; migration around 30 appears negligible in administrative data.  

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
T1: Cohort effects (men born in 1956 vs 1961 may differ).  
 • Use very narrow age windows (e.g. 28–31) and include age-in-years fixed effects.  
 • Show placebo differences in ROC and in earlier LFS years (event-study graph).  

T2: Selective migration into/out of Québec near age 30 to exploit benefits.  
 • Check inter-provincial mobility flows in SCF and Census mobility questions; adjust for province of birth.  
 • Estimate model on “non-movers in past 5 yrs” as robustness.  

T3: Measurement error in age (age-heaping).  
 • Plot histogram of single-year ages; smooth except the typical “age 30” bump?  
 • Run McCrary test; if excess mass exists, re-estimate excluding 30 exactly and using 29.5 cutoff with LFS 5-yr cohorts.  

5. R Code Outline  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# Load libraries
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional DiD/RD
library(ggplot2)
library(sandwich)
library(rdrobust)

#----------------------------
# 1. Load and merge Census data
#----------------------------
c86 <- fread("census_1986_qc_roc.csv")  # pre
c91 <- fread("census_1991_qc_roc.csv")  # post
census <- rbindlist(list(c86, c91), idcol = "year_dummy")
census[, year := fifelse(year_dummy==1, 1986L, 1991L)]

#----------------------------
# 2. Sample restrictions
#----------------------------
census <- census[sex=="M" &
                 educ=="<HS" &
                 children==0 &
                 age >=25 & age <=39]

#----------------------------
# 3. Key variables
#----------------------------
census[, post   := (year==1991)]
census[, qc     := (province=="QC")]
census[, age30p := (age>=30)]
# Triple interaction = treatment intensity
census[, treat  := qc*post*age30p]   # for ease of interpretation

# Outcomes
census[, employ := (current_week_employed==1)]
census[, hrs    := weekly_hours]
census[, weeks  := weeks_worked_last_year]
census[, livepar:= (lives_with_parents==1)]
census[, married:= (marital_status %in% c("Married","Common-law"))]

#----------------------------
# 4. Main triple-diff regression
#----------------------------
fe_formula <- employ ~ qc*post*age30p | age + province*year   # fixed effects
main <- feols(fe_formula, data = census, cluster = ~province*age)
summary(main)

#----------------------------
# 5. Local bandwidth robustness (27-33)
#----------------------------
local <- census[age>=27 & age<=33]
local_main <- feols(fe_formula, data = local, cluster = ~province*age)
summary(local_main)

#----------------------------
# 6. Visual RD (1986, Québec only)
#----------------------------
pre_qc <- census[year==1986 & qc==1]
rdplot(pre_qc$employ, pre_qc$age - 30)  # rdrobust graph
```

The same code block can be re-run for other outcomes. Additional robustness: replace `qc` with province FE and allow province-specific linear age trends; or use LFS monthly micro data, estimating an event-study:  

```r
feols(employ ~ i(rel_month, age30p, ref=-1) | province + rel_month + age, data=lfs_sub)
```  

6. Expected Results  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic theory (and U.S. AFDC evidence) predicts that higher unconditional cash transfers reduce labour supply for liquidity-unconstrained males.  

Prior: A discontinuity of +CA\$322/month (145 %) should cut employment of low-skill childless men by perhaps 5–10 p.p. (baseline ≈ 70 %). Hours conditional on work may fall slightly (1–2 hrs/wk). Living with parents likely rises (1–3 p.p.). Marriage probably falls modestly (<1 p.p.). Eliminating the gap in 1989 should produce effects of opposite sign roughly half these magnitudes given adaptation and partial take-up.  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment  
--------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: No manipulation of running variable (age) ………………… 1  
C2: Continuity of covariates at cutoff pre-policy ……………… 1  
C3: Parallel evolution of discontinuity in control provinces … 0.8  
C4: No concurrent Québec age-specific reforms ……………… 0.7  
C5: Sufficient power & bandwidth choice well justified …… 0.9  

Overall score ≈ 4.4/5 → design appears highly credible.
